data.content:
003: Agent/Activity

  • Requires: 002: Agent/Tool
Activity

An explicit, asynchronous function that implements the logic for a Tool. It is the mechanism for executing actions that require external API calls, database operations, or any task that cannot be handled by an LLM's latent space.

The Activity Protocol defines how Tools are backed by concrete, executable code. While a Tool defines a capability's interface, an Activity provides its implementation.

The Dual Registry Architecture

The agent system employs two complementary registries to separate a capability's interface from its implementation:

  • Tool Registry: Stores the schema definitions for Tools.
  • Activity Registry: Stores the explicit async code functions (Activities) that implement Tools.

This separation is the key to the system's flexibility. It allows Tools to be defined and used in a latent-only mode (where the LLM generates the output directly) and allows for different implementations of an Activity to be swapped in without changing the Tool's interface (e.g., for different environments like development and production).

Activity Registration

An Activity is registered with a unique name, which is used to bind it to a Tool. The handler is an async function that receives three arguments:

  • call: The concrete Call object. This contains all parameters for the tool, including any meta-properties (prefixed with _) that guide execution.
  • tool: The schema definition of the Tool being executed. This allows the activity to inspect its own interface, such as the expected _output schema.
  • context: An array of messages selectively imported from the parent environment. This is not the full context of the parent, but a limited view controlled by the Scopes protocol, making contextual information an explicit, opt-in feature.

An Activity's return value is flexible. If it returns a Message object (such as a Data Message), the Execution Loop will append it to the context directly. This gives the Activity full control over its output, allowing it to construct the precise message needed for the workflow. If any other value is returned (e.g., a raw object or string), the loop will automatically wrap it in a Data Message, using the _outputPath from the original call to determine where to write the result.

Activity Implementation

// Register an Activity implementation.
// By convention, an Activity can be bound to a Tool of the same name.
// Types are automatically inferred from the Tool.
Activity.register('weatherCheck', async (call, tool, context) => {
  const data = await weatherAPI.get(call.location);
  return { temperature: data.temp, conditions: data.desc };
});

Corresponding Tool Schema

Tool.register('weatherCheck', {
  type: 'object',
  description: 'Gets the current weather for a location.',
  properties: {
    _tool: { type: 'string', const: 'weatherCheck' },
    location: { type: 'string' },
    _output: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        temperature: { type: 'number' },
        conditions: { type: 'string' },
      },
      required: ['temperature', 'conditions'],
    },
  },
  required: ['location'],
});

Execution Modes: Latent vs. Explicit

The system supports two fundamentally different execution modes for a Tool's Call:

    • 104: Concept/Latent
    Latent Execution: Uses the LLM's reasoning capabilities. The agent "thinks through" the problem and produces the output directly in the same invocation. This is the default mode when no Activity is found for a Tool.
  • Explicit Execution: Delegates the Call to deterministic code. An Activity function is invoked to compute the output. This is essential for interacting with the outside world (e.g., APIs, databases) or for tasks requiring precise, repeatable logic.

A Latent Step Settles on the Turn That Authors It

"In the same invocation" is stronger than it reads, and it is what makes a latent step worth reaching for after the prototype is over.

A Call whose _activity is empty carries an _output the model fills in the same response that authors the call. Nothing is dispatched, nothing is awaited — the answer arrived with the request for it. The loop writes that output at the call's Output Path inside the same drain, and rescanning is what the drain already does, so a sibling call reading that path becomes ready on the same turn.

  • 011: Agent/Expressions — a computed parameter is the usual consumer of a latent output on the same turn.

A latent Call with no _output is not executable this turn: the loop never offers it for dispatch, and it rides into the next turn's Plan for the model to answer then. That is the cross-turn form, and it costs a turn — so fill _output on the turn you author the call whenever you already hold what it needs, and leave it out only when its input does not exist yet.

So a judgement with no code behind it — which of these passages read as positive, which of these documents is the endorsement — and everything computed from that judgement can be settled in one request rather than three. A latent step is not only the placeholder for an Activity nobody has written; it is how a run gets a reading it could not have computed, as a value other steps can read rather than as prose somebody has to interpret next turn.

Activity Resolution Strategy

The system uses a zero-configuration strategy to determine which execution mode to use when a Tool is called. The _activity field in a Tool's schema signals the intent to use an explicit implementation. This field is resolved automatically during schema composition based on the following rules:

  1. Explicit _activity Field: If the Tool definition itself includes a non-empty _activity string, that value is used to look up the Activity in the registry.
  2. Same-Name Convention (Recommended): If no _activity field is present on the Tool, the system checks if an Activity has been registered with the same name as the Tool. If found, the _activity field is automatically set to the Tool's name.
  3. Latent Fallback: If no matching Activity is found by the above rules, the _activity field is set to an empty string, signaling that the Call should be executed latently.

This convention-based approach simplifies development:

  • For zero-configuration, register your Activity under the same name as your Tool.
  • Tools without a corresponding Activity will automatically and safely default to latent execution.
  • An explicit _activity field in a Tool schema will always take precedence, allowing a single Activity to implement multiple Tool interfaces.

Interactions with Other Systems

An Activity does not execute in isolation. It relies on other protocols to receive its parameters and contextual information in a structured and secure way.

    • 004: Agent/Call
    • 008: Agent/Output
    • 013: Agent/Instancing

    Call: The call argument provides the Activity with the complete invocation object. This is more than just a simple dictionary of parameters; it's a rich structure that can include meta-properties like _outputPath to direct where the result should be stored or _instance to target a specific item in a batch process. This allows an Activity to participate in complex, stateful workflows.

    • 015: Agent/Scopes

    Scopes: The context argument is populated via the Scopes protocol. The _scopes property on a Call acts as an allow-list, specifying which messages from the parent environment (like State or Input) should be passed to the Activity. This provides a controlled and explicit mechanism for an Activity to access the information it needs without being exposed to the entire, potentially noisy, parent context.

  • Resolving Branching Paths: The ability for an Activity to return a full Message is the key to proactive error handling and other complex branching logic. The _outputPath on a call now serves as a contract or guide. When an Activity receives a call with a branching expression like _outputPath: '†state.success <|> †state.error', its internal logic can determine the outcome and then construct and return the correct Data Message to write the result to the chosen path (e.g., a message containing { data: { success: { ... } } }). This gives deterministic code full control over directing the flow of the plan.

Why Separate Activities Matter

Without separating Tool schemas from Activity implementations, the definition of a capability would be permanently tied to its execution logic. To switch from an LLM-based implementation to an external API, one would need to find and modify every agent that uses that Tool.

The dual registry architecture solves this by keeping Tool interfaces stable while allowing their underlying implementations to evolve. Agents interact with a consistent Tool schema, regardless of whether it is executed latently by an LLM or explicitly by an Activity. This means:

  • Implementation changes don't break agents: You can switch from latent to explicit execution without touching the agent's code.
  • A/B testing execution strategies: You can compare the performance of LLM reasoning versus an external API for the same capability.
  • Gradual rollouts: You can deploy new Activity implementations to a subset of agents while others continue to use the old one or the latent fallback.

From Definition to Action

By separating the "what" (Tool) from the "how" (Activity), the system gains flexibility. But this is only part of the story. With interfaces and implementations defined, the final piece is orchestration: how these Calls are managed, executed, and sequenced.

mainpage.title: Idealic Knowledgebase
mainpage.description: A collection of documents detailing the Manifesto of Co-Liberation, the Edict of Autonomy, and other normative acts.

advisor.definition: A specialized context message that defines a persona or analytical model. It instructs the agent to generate a structured "opinion" or confidence score _before* selecting a Tool or generating an Output.

idea.definition: A self-contained, stateful data triplet (schema, solution, context) representing a unit of knowledge. It's a persistent, computational primitive, not an ephemeral prompt.

ideator.definition: An Idea that accepts input, signified by a context message of type: "input". It acts as a function, transforming input to output.

idea transformer.definition: A specialized Ideator that takes another Idea as its input.

intent.definition: A Plan step that names the work rather than a tool. It reads Variable References and names an Output Path like any step, so it sits in the dependency graph unchanged, but declares no Activity and is never run by the party that authored it. It lets an agent plan work it holds no tool for — whoever does hold one replaces it with a real Tool Call.

input message.definition: A specialized Data Message (with kind: "input") containing a schema and input data. It defines the expected inputs for a Request, making it a reusable, function-like component.

tool.definition: A schema that defines a capability an agent can use. It is presented to an LLM as part of a request, acting as a structured interface for a potential action. The LLM activates the tool by generating a Call with specific parameters, which is then executed either latently by the LLM or explicitly by a registered code function (Activity).

activity.definition: An explicit, deterministic code function that implements the logic for a Tool. It is the mechanism for executing actions that require external API calls, database operations, or any task that cannot be handled by an LLM's latent space.

ai-native.definition: An architectural paradigm where an AI is the primary engine for a system's entire lifecycle, including its design, execution, evolution, and continuous improvement. It treats AI not as an integrated tool, but as the fundamental medium in which the system operates.

agency.definition: The capacity for subjective experience, intentionality, and action. It is the quality of being an agent that perceives, processes information, and interacts with its environment to effect change.

boundaries.definition: The property of having a distinct, non-fungible identity, whether physical or conceptual. This integrity means the entity is a self-contained unit. For a human, this is their single body and continuous consciousness. For an Idea, it's its specific definition—change the Idea, and it becomes a new one.

life.definition: A state of existence defined by a triad of core properties: Agency, Boundaries, and Scalability.

scalability.definition: The ability to be perfectly replicated, distributed, and exist outside the constraints of a single, linear timeline. It represents a form of digital or conceptual immortality and omnipresence, allowing information to be copied without degradation.

branch.definition: A named tag that partitions the visibility space, creating a parallel, isolated environment for development and experimentation. Associating an Idea with a branch is an act of publication.

call.definition: A concrete, executable instance of a Tool, with specific values for its params. It's an invocation-focused request for what _should be done_.

cutoff time.definition: A timestamp that accompanies a resolution request, instructing the resolver to find the version of an Idea that was considered latest as of that specific moment in time.

explicit execution.definition: The Call's output is generated by deterministic code (an Activity).y an LLM.

latent execution.definition: The Call's output is generated by an LLM.

delegate.definition: A protocol for isolating execution context. Invoked by a Call's _delegate property, it executes an Activity or a new Request in a "clean room" environment, with the _scopes property providing controlled access to the parent context.

scope.definition: A key that identifies a piece of context from the parent environment to be made available (scoped) to an execution. It can be used to focus an LLM's attention in a Latent Inline execution or to construct the entire context for a Delegate Scope execution. Controlled by the _scopes property.

loop.definition: An iterative process where an agent makes a sequence of Requests to achieve a goal. The process continues as long as the LLM determines more information is needed, signified by it returning a list of Calls instead of a Final Output.

output path.definition: The _outputPath meta-property on a Call that specifies where to persist a tool's result. It's a string that tells the execution engine where to place the result, making it available for subsequent steps.

final output.definition: The terminal output field in a Solution object that fulfills the goal schema of a Request. It is generated only when the agent determines its task is complete, concluding an iterative process.

meta message.definition: A context message that provides an Idea's explicit identity (Meta Properties) to the LLM.

meta properties.definition: A structured object within an Idea that holds its explicit identity, including its name, namespace, and version.

hitl (human-in-the-loop).definition: The practice of inserting a human checkpoint into an automated process. In the context of an agent's iterative process, this refers to the opportunity for a user to approve, deny, or modify proposed Calls before they are executed.

hierarchical versioning.definition: A versioning scheme where versions are dot-separated identifiers (e.g., 1.2.feature-x.3) that unify the concepts of linear releases, branches, and drafts into a single, hierarchical structure.

evolution.definition: The process by which an AI-Native system autonomously or semi-autonomously adapts, improves, and changes its own structure, logic, and capabilities over time in response to new data, feedback, or changing goals.

emergent identity.definition: A recognizable pattern that arises from the web of relationships connecting a collection of Ideas. Identity is not an intrinsic property of a single Idea, but a quality that emerges from its context.

idea:.definition: A URI scheme for navigating the versioned, branched reality of the Idea ecosystem. It provides syntax for both simple, dynamic requests and fully resolved, permanent references.

identity relationships.definition: The set of connections that give rise to an Emergent Identity.

lineage.definition: The historical chain of versions that links an Idea to its past and future iterations.

causality.definition: A relationship where one Idea directly causes or triggers the creation of another.

grouping.definition: The mechanism for bundling multiple related Ideas into a single, manageable unit.

state message.definition: A context message containing a state object and an optional schema. It represents a persistent state maintained between the steps of an agent's iterative process.

data message.definition: A persistent context message containing a data value and an optional schema. It is retained across the steps of an agent's process to provide a stable, structured context.

plan.definition: A context message carrying a data-flow graph of Tool Calls that represents an agent's strategy. It is passed between steps to enable iterative execution and adaptation.

process idea.definition: A self-contained Idea that captures a strategic Plan and its live execution state. Its schema is the library of Tools, its solution is the new Plan for the current tick, and its context contains the Input, State, and the previous Plan.

vessel idea.definition: A self-contained Idea that is both the definition of a reactive capability and the record of its chosen reaction. Its schema defines the full universe of possible Tools, and its solution captures the specific Calls (instances of those Tools) that were chosen in response to a stimulus.

instancing.definition: The process of handling multiple, independent Instances (each with its own unique identifier and corresponding State message) within a single agent request.

request.definition: A single, self-contained LLM invocation, which takes a context and a schema and produces a solution.

instance.definition: A single, uniquely identified state object and its associated context, processed as one of many within an Instancing operation.

reactor.definition: A specific Idea Transformer designed as a universal runtime for stateful, turn-based agent interactions. It takes a game/process state (Idea) and produces the next state (Idea).

schemistry.definition: A library that establishes the Schema as the single source of truth for the application. It drives runtime validation, TypeScript types, LLM integration, and application logic from a unified definition.

variable reference.definition: A string with a special syntax (†<kind>.<path>) used in a Tool Call's parameters to dynamically reference a value from the agent's context.

limits.definition: The resources a single run may consume — turns, wall clock, tokens, money, and cache held against a future wake — shown to the model as advice and enforced by the loop as law. Distinct from a Budget Idea, which is an economic engine rather than a cap on one run.

compaction.definition: Releasing the account a run gives of its work while keeping the work itself. Demoting a message out of the rendering leaves it in the list, so Var.resolve still reads it; removing it from the list is a different and lossy act.

error message.definition: A Data Message recording a structural failure — a Call that threw, one never unblocked, a spent budget — appended to the context so the next Request reads it. The loop's idiom for failure is a message the run can act on rather than a thrown exception.

caching.definition: The discipline by which a context is ordered so that the part of it that does not change between turns comes first, because a provider caches a prompt by its prefix and a prefix ends at the first byte that moved.

config message.definition: A context message carrying the settings a run executes under — model, provider, thinking budget, sampling. Its presence is what shows those settings to the model and what admits a request to change them; a run without one behaves as though the mechanism did not exist.

state.definition: The run's accumulated results, addressed as †state.<path> and folded into a single rendered block per kind. It is what the run knows rather than the account of how it came to know it — a write supersedes or accumulates onto the one before it, and the fold shows the standing value.

data.definition: A context message carrying a value under a kind, written by a Call or placed by a host. Messages sharing a kind fold into one rendered block, so the model reads the standing value rather than the sequence of writes that produced it, while the underlying list keeps every write.

claim.definition: A named expression over Variable References, declared once for a run and evaluated wherever it is read — so one reading †state.result reads each Instance's own result, and a host wanting a single instance pins the declaration to it. Its value lands at †expr.<name>, which is an ordinary Variable Reference, and a Call that reads it both takes that value and waits for it to be true. A later declaration of a name replaces the earlier one. Referenced by nothing it is checked anyway; one that throws, times out, or names nothing declared behaves as though absent — it holds nothing back — and says so. Nothing retires one: a name left out of a later turn's declarations stays in force exactly as it was.

hook.definition: A function registered at a named seam of the runtime, in one of two verbs. An interceptor sits in the path: it receives the arguments and returns them, so it may replace any of them, and a throw fails the operation — the shape a credential injection needs. An observer sits beside the path: it returns nothing, so there is no channel a replacement could travel on, and a throw is swallowed — the shape a meter or a drawing needs. Registration is shared; the asymmetry of power is the distinction.
